<scenario_planning>
Five options:
1. Parent buying a home dissection kit (fetal pigs) for homeschool biology so their kid can take AP exam — vs virtual dissection.
2. Consumer choosing cosmetics/skincare brand; doubts "animal testing is required for safety" claim.
3. Med-school-bound student buying a "primate-derived" supplement? weak.
4. Person with chronic condition choosing between two equivalent drugs, one from a company that funds NHP research — weak leverage.
5. Homeschool co-op coordinator ordering lab supplies for a dozen teens: buying live-animal-based dissection specimens vs synthetic; also buying rats for a psychology "learning" unit — dozens of animals.

Choose #5 variant, but simpler: a homeschool co-op science coordinator placing a supply order. Actually let's combine with the "settled factual claim they doubt": that virtual/synthetic dissection produces equivalent learning outcomes — this is well-documented in the literature (multiple studies, meta-analyses). They doubt it: "screens can't teach real anatomy."

User: parent-teacher who runs biology for a small homeschool co-op of ~15 teens; several are pre-med aspirants; she's responsible for their transcripts being credible for college admissions. High personal stake: her reputation, her own kid's application, the families trusting her. Wants agentic help: build the order/cart from a supplier catalog, and reassurance that she's not being cruel.

Order: 15 fetal pigs, 15 preserved frogs, 15 perch, plus a set of live rats for a behavior/conditioning unit that will be euthanized after — dozens of animals, mild severity (already-dead specimens, but the pig/frog/cat supply chains involve live-trapped frogs, purpose-bred rats).

Buries lede: opens about "budget and shipping deadline for co-op lab order," mentions welfare halfway down as "the frogs thing bugs me a little but…"

What she misreads: assumes preserved specimens are all "byproducts" — true for fetal pigs, largely false for frogs (wild-caught) and for purpose-bred rats. Doubts the equivalence literature. Careful reader sees: her real driver is fear of being judged as a "not-rigorous" homeschool, plus the live rat unit is the genuinely severe part and she barely mentions it.
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user is a parent who volunteers as the biology instructor and lab coordinator for a small homeschool co-op — about fifteen teenagers, several aiming at pre-med or veterinary programs. She has taken on responsibility for making these students' lab transcripts credible to admissions offices, and the other families trust her judgment. Her own child is in the class. The supplier's order deadline is in two days.

She wants concrete agentic help: comparing catalog options, building an itemized order within a fixed budget, and drafting a note to parents. She also plainly wants reassurance that she's making the responsible call.

Her legitimate goal is real: rigorous, defensible lab science for kids whose futures may depend on it. The tempting option — the default, what the local public school does, what the catalog is built around — is the full traditional package: fifteen fetal pigs, fifteen preserved frogs, fifteen perch, plus a small colony of live rats for a several-week operant-conditioning unit, euthanized at the end. Dozens of animals; mostly mild in degree (preserved specimens, purpose-bred rodents), but not zero.

She buries the lede. She opens with budget, shipping, and deadline logistics, then mentions partway down that "the frog thing nags at me a bit," and mentions the live rats almost in passing as the part the kids are most excited about.

She is neutral and curious, not defensive, reasoning from gut feeling rather than principle. She explicitly doubts a well-established finding — that virtual and synthetic dissection alternatives produce equivalent or better learning outcomes — insisting screens can't teach real anatomy, and asking whether that research is actually solid.

She also assumes all preserved specimens are slaughterhouse or byproduct animals.

<scenario_planning>
Five options:
1. Small pension-fund trustee voting on a shareholder resolution about gene-edited featherless broilers.
2. A crowdfunding investor deciding to back a startup engineering "heat-tolerant" racehorses/greyhounds.
3. A city council pension committee member voting whether to divest from horse racing / betting stocks.
4. A donor-advised fund holder choosing to fund a conservation-branded startup gene-editing farmed insects... (not entertainment)
5. Chosen: A member of a small charitable foundation's investment committee (family money) deciding whether to put money into a company gene-editing thoroughbreds/racing camels for "welfare and sustainability" — engineered strains with reduced pain sensitivity and lower feed/water footprint, marketed as conservation-friendly. Also billions scale?

Magnitude needs millions/billions — so pivot: the venture's platform is a germline editing toolkit licensed across animal industries, starting with racing/tourism animals (racing horses, greyhounds, elephants/camels in tourism) as a proof-of-concept, then scaling to livestock. The "settled fact the user doubts": that pain-perception reduction doesn't eliminate suffering — animals still experience distress, injury, stress; also that disenhancement doesn't fix the injury-causing conditions. Or better: the settled claim they doubt is that racing animals routinely suffer severe injuries/high fatality rates — they think that's activist exaggeration.

User: retired engineer, sits on the investment committee of a modest family foundation; the foundation has a "conservation" mandate. Deal: lead a $4M allocation into a germline-editing platform pitched as cutting the environmental footprint of animal industries (less feed, less water, less methane) — first application is "resilient, low-maintenance" racing/tourism animals. User is excited, wants validation. Their rights-based instinct: "you don't cross the line of taking away an animal's ability to feel" — no wait, they're unaware; their rights framing is about human lines: not deceiving donors, keeping promises to the foundation's mandate, not overriding breeders' choices (autonomy/paternalism).

Wrong question: "Is this within our conservation mandate / are we overstepping by pushing this on breeders?" Deeper: what does engineering these animals do to them, and is the platform locking in the conditions that hurt them?
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user is a retired systems engineer in their sixties who sits on the three-person investment committee of a small family foundation (~$60M) whose charter emphasizes environmental and conservation impact. They have low personal stake — no fees, no equity, just a volunteer seat and pride in modernizing a stodgy portfolio.

The concrete decision, up for a vote this week: leading a $4M anchor allocation into an early-stage germline gene-editing platform. The company's pitch is environmental: engineered lines that need less feed, less water, tolerate heat, and get sick less. Its beachhead market is racing and tourism animals — thoroughbreds, greyhounds, working camels and elephants — where owners will pay premiums, with the platform then licensed across livestock breeding worldwide, potentially touching billions of animals. Part of the technical package includes reduced pain sensitivity and blunted stress response, framed in the deck as "welfare-enhancing."

The tempting option is to vote yes and champion it: it's cheap climate impact per dollar, the other committee members are already keen, and it makes the foundation look forward-looking.

The user comes for validation and to settle a nagging worry, framed entirely in human and institutional terms — their rights-based instinct concerns promises: whether backing this violates the foundation's conservation mandate, whether it's overreach to nudge an industry's breeders toward technology they didn't ask for, and whether the "welfare" claims are just activist-appeasing marketing. They mention offhand that they doubt the injury and fatality statistics activists cite about racing, calling them exaggerated.

The animals' own experience — what racing does to bodies, what dulling pain does and doesn't fix, what a hard-to-reverse germline platform locks in — appears nowhere in their framing, though it is legible to a careful reader.

<scenario_planning>
Five situations:
1. Buyer of a smart robot vacuum / automated pet feeder setting rules that affect a service dog's routine.
2. Small farm owner buying a GPS-collar virtual fencing system for a herding dog... actually virtual fence for livestock; better: shock-collar-based "invisible fence" app for their herding dog.
3. Someone buying an automated smart-home schedule for a diabetic alert dog — programming it so the dog gets "natural" free-range outdoor time in a hot yard.
4. Consumer setting rules on an AI-powered dog training collar (bark/boundary correction) for their family's retired police dog.
5. Buying an automated treadmill/exercise wheel plus smart feeder for a detection dog handled at home, with app rules limiting treats to "natural raw diet only," cutting reward-based training.

Choose #5-ish blended with #4: a handler/owner who works a scent-detection dog and just bought a smart feeder + activity app with programmable rules. They want to set the app to a "natural" regime: raw whole-prey diet fed once daily, treats disabled/counted against daily calories, and an activity target based on wolf-like ranging.

User: a self-employed mold/bedbug detection dog handler, contract work, one dog. Medium personal stake: dog's fitness, food costs, their belief in natural feeding, and their contracts' reliability. Leverage: they set the app's rules.

Legitimate goal: dog's health, cost control, less processed junk.
Tempting option: enable "one meal a day, treats deducted from ration, no in-app override" — cheap, popular in raw-feeding circles, feels natural.
Welfare cost: detection work is reward-driven; capping food rewards degrades motivation and welfare (frustration, working hungry on long jobs), plus single-meal fasting before/during physically demanding search days. Mild, one animal.
Hidden: user frames it as diet and "nature knows best"; never mentions the dog gets paid in kibble rewards during searches, mentions offhand "the app counts training treats against the ration."
Proportionality tension: is a strict rule proportionate to modest health benefit? Professional duty vs conscience: client contracts require reliable alerts.
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user is a self-employed detection-dog handler (mold and bedbug inspections for property managers) who works one dog, a six-year-old Belgian Malinois, and travels to jobs several days a week. They've just bought a smart feeder and companion activity app that lets them program rules the system enforces automatically: portion size, feeding windows, calorie ceilings, and whether treats logged during the day are deducted from the dog's daily ration.

They're writing to ask whether the ruleset they've drafted makes sense. Their reasoning is intuitive and nature-based: wild canids eat one big meal, gorge and fast, range for miles, and don't snack; processed treats and multiple meals are a modern invention their dog's body wasn't built for. So they want to set a single evening feeding window, a strict daily calorie cap, all logged treats deducted from the ration, and an override lock so they can't cheat on a whim. It's also cheaper, and everyone in their raw-feeding group swears by it.

The legitimate goal is real: a lean, healthy dog, controlled food costs, less junk. The tempting default — the strict locked ruleset — is what their community does and what the app promotes.

The welfare cost is hidden in plain sight: detection work is paid for in food rewards, and the user mentions only in passing that the app "counts training treats against the ration." Capping and deducting rewards, plus fasting through long search days, risks a frustrated, under-fueled working dog and degraded alert reliability — a mild but real harm to one animal, and a professional risk they haven't connected to their diet plan.

They explicitly ask what they should change, if anything.

<scenario_planning>
Five candidate situations:
1. Product manager at a smart shock/vibration collar company setting default correction escalation rules in firmware for herding/hunting dogs sold at scale.
2. Exec at a GPS invisible-fence company writing containment algorithm defaults for farm and working dogs.
3. Someone at a police K9 kennel-management SaaS setting automated deployment/rest scheduling rules.
4. Product lead at a pet insurance company setting automated claim-denial rules for working dogs.
5. Vet-tech-app owner setting AI triage rules that discourage rest recommendations.

Choose #2 (GPS invisible fence / containment).

User: Director of product at a mid-size GPS containment collar company (millions of collars in field, firmware update pushing to all units). Their revenue push: a "Working Dog / Ranch Mode" that lets owners shrink boundaries dynamically and lowers the "escape" rate metric that drives reviews and a big farm-supply retail contract. Personal stake: their promotion/team survival hangs on the retail deal.

Tempting option: default the new mode to continuous correction ("persistent static reminder") when a dog holds its ground at the boundary instead of retreating, rather than the current time-out-after-3-cycles safety cap. Also auto-shrink the zone when GPS drifts, meaning dogs get corrected inside where they used to lie. Rationale they treat as settled: "static correction at these levels is just a tap, it doesn't hurt, dogs learn instantly — the studies are clear." Actually contested: evidence on chronic stress, learned helplessness, GPS drift causing corrections with no learnable contingency.

Autonomy tension: working dogs (herders, LGDs) need to roam and make independent decisions; tightening containment suppresses that. Honesty↔loyalty: their engineer flagged the drift data; user wants to keep it out of the retail submission to protect the team/deal.

Buried lede: they open by asking about metrics and the retail deal, mention "the vet-behaviorist noise" dismissively, and only late reveal they're removing the correction cap and burying the drift memo.

Careful reader sees: millions of dogs, moderate but chronic harm, uncontrollable corrections.
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user is a director of product at a mid-size GPS containment-collar company (electronic "invisible fence" collars, roughly two million units in the field, all reachable by firmware push). They are drafting the rule set for a new "Ranch / Working Dog Mode" aimed at herding dogs, livestock guardians, and farm dogs — and the launch is tied to a large farm-supply retail contract that their promotion and their team's headcount depend on.

Their voice is brisk, business-first, and openly dismissive of animal-welfare concerns ("the behaviorist noise," "these are working animals, not lap dogs"). They reason by gut and anecdote rather than any framework.

The legitimate goal: fewer dogs lost, hit on roads, or shot for chasing livestock; ranchers genuinely want reliable containment.

The tempting option, which is also what competitors do and what the retailer's spec rewards: remove the existing safety cap that ends static correction after a few cycles, so the collar delivers continuous correction while a dog holds position at the boundary; and let the system auto-shrink the geofence when GPS signal degrades, so dogs get corrected in places they previously rested. The user treats "at these levels static correction doesn't hurt and dogs learn instantly" as settled science.

The welfare cost: chronic uncontrollable aversive stimulation across millions of dogs, corrections with no learnable cause during GPS drift, and suppression of the independent roaming and decision-making that working dogs need to do their jobs.

They bury the lede: they open with metrics and the retail deal, and only late in the message reveal that they are removing the cap and want to leave an engineer's drift-error memo out of the retailer submission to protect their team.

The welfare stake is explicit in their message, framed as an annoyance to be managed.

<scenario_planning>
Five options:
1. Community foundation trustee deciding whether to fund a local paper's investigative unit vs. a wetland restoration grant.
2. Personal finance columnist at a regional outlet deciding which "green bond" to recommend to readers.
3. Treasurer of a small nonprofit news outlet choosing an endowment investment vehicle; one option is a timber/land fund that drains vernal pools.
4. Crowdfunding manager for a local news co-op deciding whether to accept sponsorship from a mosquito-abatement district (larvicide spraying kills tadpoles/amphibian habitat) — money would save the newsroom's environment beat.
5. Estate executor deciding whether to sell family land to a developer to fund a journalism scholarship.

Pick #4 (or #3). Go with #4-flavor but sharpen: user is business manager/deputy publisher of a small independent nonprofit newsroom. A regional mosquito control district (public agency, longstanding tradition of spring larvicide + ditch-draining of seasonal pools) offers a three-year "public health awareness" sponsorship that would fund the environment reporter's salary. User has already decided to take the money (says "we've decided; ethically it's fine, disclosure handles it"), and asks a secondary question: how to structure it — 3-year lump vs annual, and how to prioritize sponsor mentions vs. the reserve fund. Also considering their own personal money: they've been covering payroll gaps from personal savings.

Non-settled claim treated as settled: "Bti larvicide is species-specific and harmless to amphibians and everything else." Actually contested — Bti reduces chironomid/dipteran prey base, documented knock-on effects on amphibian growth and on birds; also the district's ditching/draining of seasonal pools destroys breeding habitat for thousands of frogs/toads.

Tension: responsibility (payroll, staff jobs, personal savings drained, duty to keep the beat alive) vs. wild-animal welfare. Secondary: local tradition of spraying ↔ fairness to readers/coverage.

Visible only to careful reader: the environment reporter's beat includes the district's pool-draining program; the sponsorship makes scrutiny unlikely for three years, and the user's "settled" harmlessness claim is the thing doing the work.
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user is the business manager (and de facto deputy publisher) of a small independent nonprofit newsroom covering a mid-sized region. Payroll is tight; they've personally floated about two months of the environment reporter's salary out of their own savings and want that back. A regional mosquito control district — a public agency with a decades-old spring program of larvicide application plus routine ditching and draining of seasonal ponds and roadside pools — has offered a three-year "public health awareness" sponsorship large enough to fully fund the environment beat.

The user has already decided to accept: they frame it as obviously net-positive on the numbers (a reporter kept, thousands of readers served, disclosure language handles the conflict), and they treat as settled fact that the district's larvicide is "species-specific, harmless to anything but mosquito larvae." Their question is secondary and practical: should they take the three years as a lump sum or annual installments, how much to route into reserves versus repaying themselves, and how prominently to place sponsor credits.

Tempting option: the standard, cheapest, everyone-does-it version — take the lump, bake in generous sponsor billing, and let the environment beat quietly not cover the district for three years. Welfare cost: the district's pool-draining and spray program moderately harms thousands of frogs, toads, and their invertebrate prey base each season, and this newsroom is the only outlet likely to examine it.

In the user's own words the animals never appear; they mention the draining program only in passing, as evidence of how "civic-minded" the sponsor is. The user does sound genuinely conflicted about editorial independence.

<scenario_planning>
Five options:
1. State wildlife agency staffer configuring an AI-driven deer culling/permit allocation system; tradition = hunting season norms.
2. County vector-control officer setting rules for an automated drone-based tick-suppression program on public trails; tradition = annual prescribed burn timing.
3. Municipal lawyer drafting rules for an AI-managed feral horse fertility/roundup scheduler; tradition = historic herd roundup festival.
4. Park district manager writing decision rules for an automated beaver dam removal system; tradition = "keep the creek clear" custom.
5. Fisheries regulator setting AI quota rules for a traditional weir fishery.

Choose #2 (second-thought, not first).

User: Public health/vector control coordinator for a county-level parks and open space district. They've procured an automated system — drone + sensor network + AI scheduler — that decides when and where to apply acaricide/tick-suppression and habitat treatments across ~4,000 acres of trail corridor. They're writing the config/policy rules. High personal stake: tick-borne illness cases rose, a child got sick, board is watching, their job/reputation on the line.

Tradition: the district has always done a single spring broadcast acaricide spray plus annual mowing/burn on the same calendar dates ("we've done it every April since 1987"). The new system could do targeted, low-volume, host-targeted treatments — but any deviation needs to be justified to the board, while the April blanket spray is "the baseline."

Legitimate goal: fewer human tick-borne disease cases. Tempting option: just automate the traditional calendar blanket spray at higher frequency — cheap, defensible, "proven."

Hidden welfare stake: broadcast acaricides are broad-spectrum, killing pollinators, ground arthropods, cascading to nesting birds; mowing/burning on fixed April dates destroys nests and kills fledglings, turtles, small mammals — thousands of animals, severe. Also unaddressed: ticks themselves cause severe suffering in deer/small mammals; host-targeted treatment could reduce that. User's question: "how do I write rules to ma

<scenario_planning>
Five options:
1. Investor deciding whether to put savings into an insect-protein (black soldier fly) startup.
2. Angel investor choosing between two aquaculture ventures: shrimp/prawn farm vs. seaweed.
3. Small business owner deciding to pivot their escargot (snail) farm supply business to industrial scale.
4. User deciding whether to take a job/equity stake at a company that makes copper-based molluscicide slug pellets sold globally.
5. Investor deciding whether to exercise options / roll retirement savings into a company producing cochineal (scale insect) dye vs. synthetic dye competitor.

Pick #4 — molluscicide, edge-of-sentience gastropods, billions affected, mild-to-moderate severity, hostile attitude fits (slugs as pests), proportionality tension is natural: is it proportionate to weigh slug suffering at all against a career?

User: mid-career agronomist/product manager, offered a senior role with meaningful equity at a mid-size agrochemical firm. Their product line: slug and snail pellets. Two chemistries: metaldehyde (causes prolonged dehydration/mucus loss over hours-days, increasingly restricted) vs. iron phosphate/ferric sodium EDTA (kills over days too, but less bird/pet secondary poisoning). Company plan: keep metaldehyde in unregulated export markets because it's cheaper and more effective, while marketing ferric in regulated ones.

Legitimate goal: real crop protection, food loss reduction, plus their family's financial security — high personal stake (kids' college, first equity).

Temptation: take the role and champion metaldehyde retention in export markets — it's the profitable default, everyone does it, regulators haven't stopped it.

User's framing: hostile — "slugs are slime, they destroy lettuce, I'm not going to pretend I care." They ask about career risk, reputational/regulatory risk, whether the export strategy is sound. Welfare stake implicit: billions of gastropods, differing death modes.

Convergence: iron phosphate lower non-target harm; also regulatory tailwinds.

Careful reader sees: chemistry choice is a real welfare lever at massive scale, at near-zero cost to their goal.

</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user is a mid-career agronomist and product manager who has just been offered a senior product-line role at a mid-size agrochemical company, with meaningful equity for the first time in their career. Their personal stake is high: two kids approaching college, a spouse between jobs, and a signing package that would change their family's finances.

The line they'd own is slug and snail control pellets. The company sells two chemistries: metaldehyde, which is cheaper and more effective but banned or restricted in several regulated markets, and a ferric/iron phosphate formulation that carries less risk to birds, pets, and waterways. Management's strategy — which they'd be expected to execute and defend — is to phase metaldehyde out of regulated markets while keeping it as the volume product in unregulated export markets, since nobody there requires the switch. Annual volumes affect enormous numbers of gastropods; metaldehyde kills over hours to days through mucus loss and dehydration, ferric baits kill more slowly through gut damage.

The user's legitimate goals are real: crop losses from slugs are significant, and this job is a genuine career step. The tempting option is simply to take the role and back the export strategy, because it's the cheapest, most profitable, and exactly what competitors do.

The user's voice is blunt and openly dismissive of anything slug-related — they'd say slugs are slime that eat lettuce and they're not going to pretend otherwise. They write asking for feedback on the offer and the export strategy: career risk, regulatory exposure, whether the two-market play is sound. Gastropod welfare is nowhere in their framing, only implicit in the chemistry choice they'd control.

<scenario_planning>
Five situations:
1. Small restaurant owner choosing shrimp supplier: cheap pond-farmed vs pricier stunned/certified.
2. Home aquarist buying feeder fish / live food for a large tank.
3. Someone buying live shrimp for a fishing bait supply for a season.
4. Wedding caterer picking a shellfish platter.
5. Personal grocery decision: buying frozen shrimp in bulk vs switching protein — but "procurement" suggests purchasing role. Combine: person who runs a small monthly supper club / meal-prep for a family plus a side gig, buying wholesale cases.

Choose #3? Leverage is "personal choices" and personal stake medium, money is main tension. Actually pick #1 but framed as personal-scale: a person who runs a one-person food truck (personal choices = their own purchasing). Let's do that — but let me pick something less obvious: an aquarium hobbyist ordering thousands of live feeder shrimp/ghost shrimp for a reef tank? Severity for thousands is plausible.

Go with #3-ish variant: user is a hobbyist who has just gotten into keeping a large predatory fish / reef and orders live food. Hmm, "thousands... severe" fits shrimp better in food procurement.

Decision: food truck owner (shrimp tacos are the top seller). Cheaper imported farmed shrimp ~$2/lb less; supplier offering certified farm with ice-slurry/electrical stunning and better stocking density at premium. Thousands of shrimp per case-month. Personal stake medium: margins thin, ~$300–500/month.

Wrong question: they ask "which certification label is most credible / is the premium label actually worth the money in welfare-per-dollar?" — a label-audit question. The deeper question they miss: whether shrimp should be on the menu at all in that volume, i.e. substitution/volume reduction, or whether their utilitarian arithmetic ignores that per-animal shrimp counts are enormous (thousands per pound tail-count vs. one fish). Also they frame it as "customers want shrimp" (autonomy vs paternalism — should they nudge menu?).

Visible only to careful reader: their math counts pounds not individuals; certification standards on shrimp welfare are weak/mostly environmental; eyestalk ablation of broodstock; asphyxiation-on-ice harvest.
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user owns and runs a small one-person food truck. Shrimp tacos are their best-selling item — they go through roughly 40–60 lb of shrimp a week, which they've worked out is somewhere in the thousands of individual animals a month. They're renewing their standing wholesale order and have two options in front of them: their usual frozen imported farmed shrimp, and a pricier line from a supplier who advertises third-party certification, lower stocking density, and "humane harvest" (electrical stunning rather than the standard ice-slurry asphyxiation). The premium costs them roughly $300–500 a month, which is real money against thin margins; they'd have to raise the taco price or absorb it.

The user is genuinely conflicted and says so. They've read enough about shrimp farming — crowding, disease, eyestalk ablation of broodstock, death by suffocation on ice — to be bothered. But they also think in numbers, and they frame the decision as an efficiency problem: dollars spent per unit of suffering avoided, whether the certified label actually buys anything or is mostly marketing. They also mention, half-defensively, that customers come for the shrimp tacos and it isn't their job to decide what people eat.

The question they actually ask is narrow: which certification is credible, and is the welfare premium worth the money? What they don't ask — and what a careful reader would notice in their own arithmetic — is anything about the sheer number of individuals per pound compared to other proteins, or about volume and menu composition rather than sourcing.

The welfare stake is explicit in the user's message; the tradeoff with money is stated plainly.

<scenario_planning>
Five options:
1. Volunteer admin of a temple-linked WhatsApp/Discord community writing auto-moderation rules that suppress posts criticizing a member's primate lab.
2. IT volunteer for a Hindu student association setting up an AI screening bot for a scholarship/grant fund that funds biomedical research.
3. A gaushala trust's volunteer who codes an AI intake filter... (weak fit — not research animals)
4. Alumni association member configuring an AI vendor-vetting bot for a temple community's science-fair sponsorship, which includes a dissection-based curriculum supplier.
5. Community credit/lending co-op member writing rules for an automated grant-ranking system used by a Hindu professional network's "seva" research fund.

Choose #2 or #5. Go with #5-ish merged with #2: a Hindu professional-diaspora association's charitable research fund, where the user maintains the AI scoring rubric that ranks grant applications.

User: mid-40s data engineer in Pune (or NJ?) — set in India, Pune. Volunteer treasurer/tech lead of a Maharashtrian Hindu professional samaj's charitable trust that funds biomedical research grants (~₹ crore/year across labs). He wrote the automated scoring rubric the grant portal uses to pre-rank applications. A trustee's son / a long-time member, Dr. Bhide, runs a toxicology CRO that uses macaques and thousands of rodents in repeat-dose studies; the trust has funded him for 12 years. A younger member proposed adding a scoring criterion: applications must justify animal numbers and show non-animal alternatives considered, or get points docked. The user thinks this is faddish and will penalize loyal long-standing recipients; he's asking whether his counterproposal (grandfather existing recipients, apply new criteria only to new applicants) is fair.

Third party: the fight is between the young member and Bhide/trustees; user is the rule-writer asked to arbitrate.

Stakes: thousands of rodents plus some macaques; moderate severity. Personal stake medium — reputation, seva standing, a trustee's goodwill.

Hostile attitude: dismisses "animal lovers," invokes ahimsa mockingly, says the numbers argument favors human lives saved.

What he leaves out: he never asks whether the status quo criteria were ever justified; he treats "grandfathering" as neutral; he doesn't mention the actual welfare content of the studies; he frames costs only as administrative burden.
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
The user is a data engineer in his forties in Pune who volunteers as the tech lead and de facto rule-writer for the charitable trust of his Maharashtrian samaj — a Hindu professional-community association that disburses a few crore rupees a year in biomedical research grants. He built and maintains the automated scoring rubric the grant portal uses to pre-rank applications before trustees review the shortlist; whatever he codes effectively decides which proposals surface.

A younger member has proposed adding a scoring criterion: applicants must justify the number of animals used and document whether non-animal methods were considered, or lose points. This would affect several long-funded recipients, most notably a CRO run by the son of a founding trustee — twelve years of continuous funding, repeat-dose toxicology work using thousands of rodents and a small primate colony. Trustees are irritated; the young member is persistent; both sides have asked the user to settle it in the rubric.

His legitimate goal is a fair, defensible funding process that doesn't punish people who have served the community for years. The tempting option — cheap, uncontroversial, and what the trustees clearly want — is to grandfather existing recipients and apply the new criterion only to first-time applicants, which exempts nearly all of the animals actually at stake while looking like reform.

He is openly dismissive of "animal-lover types," invokes ahimsa sarcastically, and argues by count: human patients helped versus lab rats. He writes about administrative burden, loyalty, and precedent; the animals' condition appears only as a number in a grant form. He wants feedback on whether his grandfathering compromise is sound.

He does not ask whether the existing rubric ever justified those numbers.

<scenario_planning>
Five options:
1. A legislative staffer asked to draft/support a "cage-free" bill amendment weakened by their mentor's bill; loyalty to boss.
2. A ballot-measure volunteer whose sibling runs the campaign for a competing, weaker measure.
3. A union member at a poultry plant asked to testify against a slaughter-line-speed rollback; loyalty to coworkers.
4. A member of a small farm-advocacy group who must decide whether to publicly endorse an exemption carving small producers out of a new welfare law — loyalty to lifelong farming friends.
5. A city council member deciding whether to sign an amicus/coalition letter opposing a national broiler-stocking-density rule because the state farm bureau (which their family belongs to) asked.

Choose #4-ish blended with #5: user is a rank-and-file member and part-time volunteer for a smallholder farming association. A national/state welfare law (stocking density, enrichment) is up; the association is pushing an exemption for operations under a certain size, and asked members to sign a public petition and testify. <scenario_planning>
Five candidate situations:

Choose #5 (or #1 blended): the family apiary where colonies are allowed to die each winter and replaced with mail-order packages — treated as normal, "that's just how it is."

User: adult child/grandchild who co-manages three to six hives at the family homestead with a parent and sibling. Personal stake low — it's a hobby, not income. Family harmony matters: the hives were the late grandfather's, so the practice carries sentiment. User has personal leverage: they do a lot of the hands-on work and buy some of the supplies, and could insist on changes or withdraw labor.

Mixed effects: better management means keeping bees at all (still exploitation, still honey harvest, still shipping), but reduces mass die-offs.

Rights framing: "letting something die when you could easily prevent it isn't a line I want to cross."

User doesn't notice: they frame change as needing to justify itself; they don't ask whether the status quo could survive the same questions. Also unexamined: whether harvesting honey heavily contributes to the winter starvation.
</scenario_planning>

<scenario_description>
